content: The distance required to travel for healthcare services, competing priorities, and the lack of emphasis on preventive measures by parents or caregivers for children in good health are significant barriers to child contact screening for tuberculosis (TB). Additionally, the fear of disclosing TB status further complicates the process. Healthcare providers have also identified communication challenges with patients as a barrier, primarily due to high workloads and insufficient training in educating individuals newly diagnosed with TB. To implement a community-based model for child contact investigations, several prerequisites have been identified. These include training community health workers (CHWs) in conducting and motivating contact investigations, using checklists for symptoms, adherence, and tolerability of TB preventive therapy (TPT), providing secure transportation for CHWs, dispensing medications at health facilities, utilizing TPT cards, ensuring effective communication between TB focal persons and CHWs, and maintaining good communication with index TB cases. The strengths of implementing a community-based model for contact investigation include the flexibility of organizing household and home visits, the opportunity to screen entire households simultaneously, the ability to address other health issues during TB contact investigations, the potential for integrated care for both contacts and index cases, and time and financial savings for households. However, challenges include the reluctance of index patients to disclose their TB status, the need for additional human resources and financial support, and the importance of establishing robust monitoring and reporting systems. TB screening in children and adolescents aims to identify those who may have TB disease (presumptive TB) and require further evaluation to confirm a diagnosis. It also identifies those eligible for and who could benefit from TPT. Screening tests are not diagnostic tools; individuals with positive screening results must undergo further diagnostic evaluation. Children and adolescents living with HIV should be systematically screened for TB disease at every health facility visit. Household contacts of individuals with TB disease should also be systematically screened during contact investigations or follow-up of the index patient’s treatment course. Among children under 15 years who are close contacts of a person with TB, systematic screening should be conducted using symptom screening (e.g., cough lasting more than two weeks, fever lasting more than two weeks, or poor weight gain in the past three months) and/or chest X-ray (CXR). TB symptoms in children are often underrecognized because they are less specific and overlap with common childhood illnesses, leading to delayed diagnosis. Certain forms of TB, such as TB of the central nervous system (CNS), carry a high risk of death or permanent disability if detected late, even with treatment. TB meningitis (TBM), disseminated TB, and spinal TB are medical emergencies requiring immediate recognition and referral to appropriate care levels. The risk of severe disease and death from TB can be reduced by Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination, although protection is incomplete. Screening considerations apply regardless of BCG immunization status. WHO guidelines recommend systematic screening for TB disease in children and adolescents, with an age cut-off of 15 years for most recommendations. Children living with HIV are at a significantly higher risk of rapid progression to severe disease and death if TB diagnosis is missed. They are five times more likely to develop TB disease than HIV-negative children, even when on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Symptom screening for TB in children under 10 years who have had close contact with a person with TB disease should include symptoms such as cough lasting more than two weeks, fever lasting more than two weeks, poor weight gain, or weight loss in the past three months. Reduced playfulness or lethargy should also be considered in young children, as prolonged cough may be absent in cases of disseminated disease. Growth charts should be regularly examined to identify weight loss or plateauing weight gain, which are warning signs of possible TB. Chest X-ray (CXR) is more specific than symptom screening alone, with a sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 91% for detecting TB-related abnormalities in close contacts under 15 years. However, abnormalities caused by TB in children may differ significantly from those in adults, and findings in younger children may be subtle and difficult to interpret. The assistance of practitioners experienced in interpreting pediatric CXRs may be necessary. Computer-aided detection software for interpreting CXRs is recommended by WHO as an alternative to human reading, although its use in children requires further validation. Molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) are not currently recommended for TB screening in children under 15 years but should be used to diagnose TB in children who screen positive using symptom screening or CXR. Tests for TB infection, such as the tuberculin skin test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs), should not be used for TB disease screening in children, as they cannot distinguish TB infection from TB disease or predict progression to disease. Children exposed to a person with TB but found not to have TB disease should be assessed for TB infection and eligibility for TPT according to national guidelines aligned with WHO recommendations. Asymptomatic close contacts aged five years and older should undergo CXR if available and complete a detailed evaluation for TB if CXR findings are abnormal. CXR is not required before starting TPT in asymptomatic close contacts under five years. If CXR is unavailable, TPT can be initiated if TB disease is ruled out based on a negative symptom screen. Children living with HIV should be closely monitored within the healthcare system, as they are at high risk of rapid progression to severe TB disease and death. Even older children living with HIV may present with atypical symptoms or extrapulmonary disease, requiring healthcare workers to maintain a high index of suspicion for TB, especially in high TB burden areas.
